blocks.text: Imagine building a skyscraper without testing the strength of each beam or the stability of each floor. Software testing ensures each 'beam' of your code is strong before the 'skyscraper' is complete.

blocks.markdown: In software engineering, testing is crucial to ensure that software behaves as expected. Testing can be divided into different levels, each serving a unique purpose. These levels are unit testing, integration testing, system testing, and acceptance testing. Understanding these levels helps in systematically building confidence in software rather than relying on hope.

blocks.title: Unit Testing
blocks.text: Unit testing focuses on testing individual components or functions of the software in isolation. It aims to validate that each unit of the software performs as expected.

blocks.title: Integration Testing
blocks.text: Integration testing evaluates the interaction between integrated units or components. It ensures that combined parts of the software work together as intended.

blocks.title: System Testing
blocks.text: System testing assesses the complete and integrated software system. It verifies that the system meets the specified requirements.

blocks.title: Acceptance Testing
blocks.text: Acceptance testing is performed to determine whether the software is ready for delivery. It is often conducted by the end-users to ensure the system meets their needs.

blocks.markdown: The test pyramid is a concept that guides the distribution of different types of tests. It suggests having many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and even fewer system tests. This structure helps in maintaining a balance between fast feedback and comprehensive coverage.

blocks.caption: The test pyramid suggests that the number of unit tests \( T_{unit} \) should be greater than the number of integration tests \( T_{integration} \), which in turn should be greater than the number of system tests \( T_{system} \).

blocks.title: Example: Applying the Test Pyramid
blocks.prompt: A software team is developing a web application. They have written 200 unit tests, 50 integration tests, and 10 system tests. How does this align with the test pyramid?

steps.text: Identify the number of tests at each level: 200 unit tests, 50 integration tests, 10 system tests.
Compare the numbers to the test pyramid structure: \( T_{unit} > T_{integration} > T_{system} \).
200 > 50 > 10, which aligns with the test pyramid's recommendation.

blocks.answer: The distribution of tests aligns well with the test pyramid, supporting fast feedback and comprehensive coverage.

blocks.caption: Comparison of different test levels by scope and purpose.

blocks.title: Example: Choosing the Appropriate Test Level
blocks.prompt: A critical bug was found in the interaction between the payment module and the order processing module of an e-commerce system. Which test level should be prioritized to address this issue?

steps.text: Identify the nature of the bug: it involves interaction between modules.
Determine the test level that focuses on interactions: Integration Testing.

blocks.answer: Integration testing should be prioritized to address the interaction issue between the payment and order processing modules.

blocks.title: Cost of Inverting the Test Pyramid
blocks.text: Inverting the test pyramid, by having more system tests than unit tests, can lead to slower feedback, higher costs, and more complex debugging processes.

points: Unit testing focuses on individual components, integration testing on combined components, system testing on the entire system, and acceptance testing on user needs.
The test pyramid guides the distribution of tests to balance fast feedback and comprehensive coverage.
Choosing the appropriate test level depends on the scope and nature of the risk.
